There is potential for cross- institute collaboration between MSU and OSU electron beam facilities, and potential users in areas including superconductor science, fusion, or fission science at MIT, Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, the DIII-D National Fusion Facility and other labs. The academic labs could focus on fundamental research and initial development while a private contractor could support production. Retention of know-how and routine maintenance suggests that the EBW equipment requires support from a full-time engineer or experienced technician: leaving the machine to be operated by students could lead to safety or equipment issues. MSU sought internal funds to buy an electron beam welder after reviewing the total cost they spent on buying electron beam welder time and sending personnel to job shops for prototyping of SRF cavities. Their approach to one-of-a-kind technical procurements, such as SRF cavities, was that they make a reference design and several prototypes, so that they can validate the reference design and optimize its fabricability and are well- informed customers when they approach industry for “mass” production. This also leads to a fairer price based on an appropriate risk allocation between the vendor and customer. For specialty SRF developments, most recently the SRF e-gun injector for LCLS-2 HE, they used the same approach to make non-mass-produced quantities in-house. MSU will currently be restricting use of the electron beam welding system to niobium welding. As a recipient of public funds, MSU is not allowed to compete with commercially available services, although there are potential avenues for collaboration with industry on research and development efforts. OSU salvaged a used PTR system from Y-12 and is negotiating refurbishment of the system. It will be used for workforce development and electron beam welding research and development for all materials including niobium and copper, but the chamber is not large enough for full-sized accelerator prototype manufacturing. High gradient AS require more time than those with conventional gradients to condition up to operating power levels. In addition, the process must be carefully performed in order to ensure no permanent damage is imparted upon the structures.
